item.title: Stigma Keeps Academics' Addictions in the Shadows
item.description:
Addiction

Stigma Keeps Academics' Addictions in the Shadows

The response to a podcast about my addiction story shouldn't surprise anyone.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Stigma surrounding addiction keeps many professors’ addictions hidden.
  • Fear of career damage stops academics from seeking support for addiction.
  • Humanizing addiction may be key to breaking this stigma in higher education.

Back in May of this year, Scott Carlson, senior writer at the Chronicle of Higher Education, wrote a story about substance abuse among college professors. As a former professor who struggled with addiction for years, I read Scott’s story with great interest. Although I’d published a memoir a couple of months prior in which I discuss addiction in academia, Scott’s article prompted me to do more.

I contacted him, and we had a thought-provoking discussion about stigma toward addiction, which exceeds stigma toward any other mental health condition. I blogged about it afterward, but that didn’t seem like enough. Fear of stigma kept me in the closet about my addiction for 25 years, and two things science tells us are that (1) academics tend to hide almost any disability at almost any cost; and (2) stigma thrives on secrecy. Reducing stigma requires people to share their stories, putting human faces on them. Not everyone, however, is in a position to do this.

I reached out to Louis Essig and Aaron Garnes, who kindly hosted me on their popular Get a Grip podcast, which explores life before, during, and after addiction. The podcast is unscripted and often raw. Guests expose their private struggles with addiction in ways fellow travelers can identify with, and in ways others without addiction can gain insight from, even if they can’t fully understand.

Almost immediately after my episode dropped, the avalanche started: emails, instant messages through Facebook and LinkedIn, and contacts through my website. It included graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, early career, mid-career, and senior faculty members struggling with substance abuse and addiction and keeping it secret—just as I had for 25 years, and just as the literature suggests. Almost everyone expressed paralyzing fear that their careers would be over and their reputations forever tarnished if they came out. Stigma runs deep in higher ed.

I’m both surprised and unsurprised by the number of academics who, in such a short time, contacted me. Surprised that so many reached out, but unsurprised that so many are affected, including, undoubtedly, many more.

This is my shortest blog post to date because I don’t know what comes next. I have another podcast to record, and a couple of public appearances in the works. I’m thinking hard about what to say. If you have ideas, please send them along.

Smart people have been working to reduce stigma toward addiction for many years. We rename disorders, compare addiction to less stigmatized diseases, and frame relapse as normal. We conduct public awareness campaigns, yet year after year, stigma just seems to increase.

We need a new approach. It’s hard to know what that might look like, but putting human faces on addiction will surely play a part. One thing's for sure: Human lives both inside and outside our profession are at stake.

item.title: A Reflection on Illness, Safety, and Adaptation
item.description:
Chronic Illness

A Reflection on Illness, Safety, and Adaptation

How to push on when chronic illness undermines our sense of safety.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic illness can undermine psychological safety, making adaptation and coping more difficult.
  • Anxiety, avoidance, and withdrawal may reflect threat responses rather than poor coping.
  • Safety, not resilience alone, may be the foundation for well-being in long-term conditions.
  • Sometimes coping means creating shelter, slowing down, and letting the storm pass.

At a recent specialist heart review, I received disappointing news about my heart function. It means new medication, further tests, and more appointments. After the brief consultation, I found myself standing in the hospital corridor, clutching a leaflet and trying to stem a tsunami of panic, confusion, and memories of past medical trauma.

While this news helps explain my increased breathlessness, exercise intolerance, and fatigue, it has also pulled the rug from beneath my feet, casting fresh uncertainty over my career, finances, plans, and goals. Advances in treatment have made much possible, but each new setback still requires adaptation.

As both a psychologist and a person living with a congenital heart condition, I have become increasingly interested in how illness can undermine our sense of safety and shape our capacity to adapt. As I focus on my own health and well-being, I find myself returning to this question to make sense of experiences that can otherwise feel overwhelming.

When Chronic Illness Steals Your Sense of Safety

Psychological safety is the sense that we are secure enough to engage with life, connect with others, regulate our emotions, and move towards what matters. When that sense of safety is disrupted, adaptation and coping become much harder.

In recent work, I have proposed that psychological safety provides a useful framework for understanding coping in long-term conditions. Across different areas of psychology, a common theme emerges: People adapt and thrive more easily when they feel safe.

Living with a chronic condition often involves persistent threats, including symptom flare-ups, healthcare encounters, medical procedures, challenges accessing care, discrimination, and repeated losses. When a condition is present from infancy, these experiences can become deeply embedded, shaping identity, trust, emotional regulation, relationships, and a fundamental sense of safety in the world. Even when treatment is effective, ongoing uncertainty and medical setbacks can leave a lasting psychological imprint.

Seen through the lens of psychological safety, resilience can look very different. What is often interpreted as poor coping may reflect an understandable response to threat. Behaviours such as anxiety, withdrawal, avoidance, or reassurance-seeking are often attempts to manage perceived threat. A patient who repeatedly misses appointments may be labelled disengaged, while someone who frequently seeks reassurance may be viewed as demanding. Yet these responses may arise from previous healthcare experiences that felt frightening, invalidating, or overwhelming. These responses can be understood as attempts to manage threat rather than signalling poor motivation or engagement.

After difficult medical news, I often notice my sense of safety begin to unravel. My world narrows, future plans become uncertain, and memories of earlier medical crises can re-emerge, making it difficult to disentangle present challenges from past trauma.

'Coorie Doon' and Let the Storm Pass

As I await further investigations and adjust to another chapter of uncertainty, I am reminded that coping sometimes involves slowing down rather than pushing forward. In Scotland, the phrase coorie doon means to settle somewhere safe and sheltered until the storm passes. During a medical crisis, the answer is not always to fight harder, think more positively, or keep going at all costs. Sometimes the task is to create enough safety to weather the storm; to coorie doon.

Grounding myself in the present and reminding myself that past medical experiences are not the same as current realities helps restore a sense of safety and possibility. For me, this involves drawing on trusted relationships, practising self-compassion, and returning to small acts of self-care, such as drawing, reading, enjoying comforting movies and music, listening to my body's signals, and allowing myself to rest. These practices help me feel steady enough to face my situation and find the strength to advocate for my care without becoming overwhelmed.

In a culture that celebrates resilience, we often overlook the foundation on which it depends. For those living with chronic illness, this may mean finding safety within themselves, in supportive relationships, or through compassionate healthcare. That sense of safety may support moving forward, or it may create the space needed to pause, rest, adapt, and recover. Healthcare can also play an important role in fostering psychological safety. Compassionate communication, validation, consistency, and genuine collaboration can all help people feel safer as they navigate health challenges. Families, communities, colleagues, and healthcare professionals all play a role in creating conditions that support adaptation and well-being. While chronic illness and uncertainty often go hand in hand, feeling safe can make it easier to continue engaging with what matters most.

item.title: Unanswered Questions in the Lindsay Clancy Case
item.description:
Law and Crime

Unanswered Questions in the Lindsay Clancy Case

The mental health effects of a potential mistrial.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Uncertainty and ambiguity often cause psychological distress.
  • Mistrials in high-profile legal proceedings may provoke strong emotional reactions.
  • Limiting social media consumption can help manage the stress of high-profile outcomes.

The high-profile Lindsay Clancy murder case has intrigued much of the American public. After five days, the jury has been unable to reach a verdict, although the presiding judge has instructed the jury to continue deliberations. Significant coverage by news and social media outlets has kept public attention high with a steady focus on a near outcome. Online outlets have even included live feeds in anticipation of a verdict. But continued lack of consensus by the jury raises the prospect of a mistrial. What if no verdict comes?

A mistrial is a judicial proceeding that is terminated without reaching a final verdict or judgment. Trials have the specific aim of providing an answer—even if contested later on appeal—for an individual facing criminal charges. The scope of evidence presented and arguments made allow a jury to reach a conclusion about innocence or guilt for the accused. For the public that may be following, a mistrial disrupts this expectation.

The aftereffects for those tuned into high-profile cases are notable. History informs what these might be. On-lookers closely following may become more polarized in their viewpoints following a hung jury. The initial mistrials declared in the murder trial of the Menendez brothers sparked widespread public disagreement about their guilt or innocence. Decades later, social media has compounded this likelihood. Distrust of some public media outlets and online content leads many to gravitate to sources that confirm their positions (“echo chambers”). Online algorithms, especially for AI-generated content, promote active engagement, including the anger that sometimes accompanies forceful online opinions.

For some, however, polarization following a mistrial is not the immediate consequence. If significant time and energy have been devoted to following a criminal court case, an empty verdict may induce a state of emotional exhaustion. The lack of an anticipated verdict after high emotional and cognitive investment may leave individuals sullen, disappointed, drained, and even cynical.

The let-down that accompanies spectator fatigue can be especially uncomfortable for people who readily identify with the content of a legal proceeding. The case of Lindsay Clancy has galvanized advocates for post-partum mental health, increasing much-needed focus on depression and psychosis among women. An equivocal outcome to the trial may be experienced as heightened anxiety and sadness when the nature of the case has high personal resonance.

How can one safeguard their mental health under such circumstances? Ambiguity and uncertainty are inherently uncomfortable but manageable as well. Acknowledging the unknown is an important first step towards recognition that although control over the conclusion of a court case is not within one’s individual scope, our emotional response often is. Social support is also critical, regardless of the verdict, when navigating the uncertainty of events in the forefront of public consciousness. Additionally, reducing one’s screen time helps mitigate depressive symptoms and self-reported stress and enhances sleep quality and perceived well-being. With rapid-fire news updates at our fingertips, restraint can be valuable.

Whatever the outcome of the Lindsay Clancy case, vocal discourse is likely to continue in the court of public opinion. Close attention to one’s mental well-being now can help buffer whatever comes next.

item.title: Supporting Our Kids and Ourselves This Back-to-School Season
item.description:
Parenting

Supporting Our Kids and Ourselves This Back-to-School Season

Give children space to grow, navigate challenges, and find their way.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Back-to-school is a transition for the whole family system.
  • Every stage and send-off looks different, but what they need underneath it looks a lot the same.
  • Supporting our children well also means looking after ourselves.

No matter what age our kids are, back-to-school season brings a shift in routines, emotions, and expectations for the whole family system. While those shifts look different at each stage, our children continue to need our support in ways that change with them. Sometimes that means holding their hand; other times, it means listening from a distance, offering perspective, or reminding them that we're here. Our role is to stay close enough that they know they belong and we're in their corner, while giving them enough space to grow, make their own choices, and find their way.

Here are a few ways to support our littles, middles, and bigs this season, along with a gentle reminder that we need to look after ourselves, too.

Supporting Our Littles

For our youngest kids, back-to-school is mostly about the unknown. They may not be able to picture the routine yet, so uncertainty can show up as big feelings over seemingly small things. Structure helps enormously here. Preparing the night before, choosing outfits, and packing bags together smooth out your mornings and build your child's own sense of capability. Small choices, like which snack to pack or what order to get ready in, give them a healthy dose of agency inside a routine that is otherwise decided for them.

Littles don't always need a long conversation about the emotional weight of change. Often, what helps most is simple information about what comes next. When will they see their sibling again? What happens after drop-off? What is for lunch? Answering the practical questions while acknowledging their feelings can help them feel safer and more settled.

Supporting Our Middles

At this stage, adolescents are building their identity outside the family system. That means new friendships, new pressures and stressors, and new ways of exploring who they are. As they move toward greater independence, our role begins to shift, too.

We don't get to choose whether our children will encounter challenges. We do, however, have opportunities to help them build the confidence they will need to navigate them before the stakes are higher.

Part of that means resisting the urge to remove every obstacle, discomfort, or consequence from their path. When we do everything for them, even with the very best intentions, we can unintentionally take away opportunities to practice problem-solving and build self-efficacy.

This is the distinction between supporting and rescuing. Supporting says, "I believe you can do this, and I'm here if you need me." Rescuing can unintentionally communicate, "I don't think you can handle this, so let me do it for you." Whenever we're able to pause before solving a problem for our children, we create another opportunity for them to discover that they are more capable than they realized. I shared more ways we can foster resilience in adolescents and teens in a previous post.

Keep making room for conversations that have nothing to do with school or what needs to get done. Show curiosity about their hobbies and interests. Share low-pressure, ear-to-ear conversations on a car ride, a walk, or while making dinner together. These moments are often where they open up the most.

Supporting Our Bigs

Sending a student off to post-secondary is its own kind of transition, for them and for us. It's a big academic, social, and emotional shift for students, and for parents and supporters, it can be a real mixed bag of emotions.

The goal also isn't to make the path easy. It's to help them trust themselves and believe they can soar, while knowing they always have somewhere safe to land.

When your student calls home overwhelmed, our instinct is to reassure: "You've got this," or "You've done hard things before." The invitation is to pause before jumping in to fix or rescue, and take your CUE:

  • Connect with genuine presence.
  • Understand what is actually going on.
  • Empower them to find one small next step.

A few phrases that can help:

  • "I believe you." You don’t have to agree with their conclusion. You're believing the feeling they're experiencing. That's what needs to be heard first.
  • "Paint me a picture. Help me understand." Instead of jumping to solutions, ask them to describe what it actually feels like. This moves the conversation from the circumstance into the experience.
  • "What I'm hearing you say is..." Reflecting back what you're hearing helps them feel understood, which is often the first step toward feeling capable again.
  • "What's one thing I can do that won't make this worse?" This gives them agency while making it clear you are there to support, not take over.

I explored the transition to post-secondary for students and their families more in a previous post.

Supporting Ourselves

We are naturally dedicated to ensuring our children have everything they need to feel safe, secure, supported, and successful. At the same time, it is important that we lean into our own outlets to process what we're feeling and take care of our well-being. One of the greatest gifts we can give to the people we love is taking good care of the person they love. When we care for our own well-being, even in small ways through things like rest, solitude, or movement, we show up with more presence, patience, and compassion for those who need us most.

Final Thoughts

There is no single right way to walk through this season, whichever stage of send-off you're in. Every household and family system is going to focus on what works for them. We don't have to have it all figured out, either. At every stage, our children are adjusting to something new, and so are we.

My final gentle invitation is this: When you see your loved ones again, let your face light up. That simple moment of joy and connection when you reunite at the end of the day, or after a semester away, lets them know they belong and matter. They aren't asking us to be perfect. They're looking for connection, understanding, and a steady presence beside them as they learn they are capable of navigating whatever comes their way. And in times when you aren't sure what the next step is, you can trust that, however this year unfolds, you will find a way through it together.

item.title: Once a Suicidal Crisis Passes, the Danger Isn’t Over
item.description:
Suicide

Once a Suicidal Crisis Passes, the Danger Isn’t Over

The week after medical discharge following a suicide attempt, risk is elevated.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • For men, the risk of suicide after discharge following an attempt is 102 times greater.
  • For women the risk is 256 times greater.
  • Elevated mood swings and more upbeat behavior can mean an attempt is imminent.

Often it’s assumed that after a person has been hospitalized for a suicide attempt, then released, the danger has diminished. In fact, the opposite is true. One study found that for men, the risk of suicide in the first week after discharge from a psychiatric hospital for an attempt is 102 times greater, while for women it’s 256 times greater.[1] A reason for this is the mistaken belief that when a person is discharged, doctors and nurses have dealt with the problem so loved ones can relax. On the contrary, loved ones need to get the person into longer-term care, such as counseling, to deal with root causes.

According to the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 77 percent of individuals who die by suicide visited their primary care physician within the past year. Forty-five percent visited their physician within the past month. Ten percent were discharged from a hospital within the past 60 days.[2]

According to a study in the journal Medical Care, 38 percent of individuals who attempt suicide visited a healthcare provider—primary care, specialty care, or emergency department—within the week before their attempt. Nearly all—95 percent—visited a healthcare provider within the preceding year.[3]

What this means is that people see physicians fairly regularly, but these visits have little or nothing to do with suicide prevention, mainly because the subject of suicide doesn’t come up. Physicians aren’t trained to ask, and people, in general, are much more comfortable talking about a physical problem than a psychological one. As a result, an opportunity is missed.

Related to this is the phenomenon whereby, after a prolonged period of depression, suicidal people exhibit elevated mood swings. This leads others to think that the danger has passed, or at least it has subsided. The upbeat attitude is misinterpreted as a sign that people are getting better, that they are feeling more optimistic about life. In fact, they are upbeat for an entirely different reason—they have made a decision to die. They have taken control of their lives after feeling out of control, and believe that the end to their pain and suffering is near.

In the immediate aftermath of someone’s release following hospitalization for a suicide attempt, everyone in that individual’s support system—family, friends, coworkers, clinicians, clergy, physicians—needs to be especially vigilant. The person’s life may depend on it.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy: Is She Our Present-Day Medea?
item.description:
Parenting

Lindsay Clancy: Is She Our Present-Day Medea?

An accused mother's trial has captured the hearts and minds of a nation.

Posted September 3, 2026

I think back to August 1980. I had a newborn baby, and at almost the same time, new mother Lindy Chamberlain accused a dingo of taking her baby from a tent in the Australian Outback. Later, she was found guilty of murdering her 9-week-old baby daughter, Azaria. This case was replete with conspiracy stories. Was she shielding her son and her husband? Did Azaria’s name mean sacrifice?

As a new first-time mom, I wanted to blame Lindy. I was high on post-birth hormones. It wasn't only about Azaria; it was about protecting my baby. I truly wanted revenge. I wanted her to rot in jail.

She did go to jail. Years later, her conviction was overturned, and she was ultimately exonerated.

Lindy Chamberlain’s name lives on in Australian folklore. An echo of this infamous Australian case is being replayed in the U.S. at this moment. I have taken the opportunity to think about how I responded to Lindy 46 years ago and how I think about Lindsay now.

Fast-forward to September 2026

The U.S. is in a frenzy.

Lindsay Clancy’s name is on everybody’s lips. She is on trial in Massachusetts on charges related to the deaths of her children, Cora (5), Dawson (3), and Callan (8 months), in January 2023. All the social media sites are clogged up with opinions, conspiracy theories, support, and venom. It’s impossible to get away from the conversation. Intense emotions, including fury, disbelief, judgement, blame, compassion, and vehement opposition, are colliding.

Up until now, I’ve been watching this media feast in astonishment as everyone is taking a bite of Lindsay’s life.

I think back to how I “knew” that Lindy was guilty and how I wasn't measured or thoughtful. I wanted Lindy to suffer. I wonder how, unlike Margo in 1980, we can have respectful and reasonable conversations without being overtaken by unbridled emotions and binary thoughts. Can this tragedy become an opportunity to reflect on our values, our compassion, our rage, and the intrusive role of the media?

Where we are at this moment in time

What everyone may be able to agree on is that this is a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. Maternal filicide has long been part of human experience. It has been represented throughout time immemorial in reality and in art forms such as drama, literature, film, and sculpture. Think Euripides’ Greek tragedy Medea, performed since 431 B.C.E.; Andrea Yates in Houston, Texas, in 2001; Lindy Chamberlain…

Of course, when a child dies, especially at the hands of his/her mother, the person who is meant to be his/her main protector, we are all rocked. We are shocked. Furious, we want blood. We cannot tolerate this rupture of the natural order. We are blinded by grief and unrestrained anger. Maybe if she’s locked up, we will be safe. Safe from our pain, our horror. Safe from our imaginings about Lindsay.

What can we learn from this?

  • We must reset how we think about mothering. We need to honor and listen to mothers’ voices. They hold our most precious resource, our children, in their hands.
  • Lindsay’s situation represents a raw truth. Mothers struggle. Life with dependent babies and children is tough. It's arguably the most demanding and difficult job going. Mothers need support to keep themselves and their children safe.
  • The behavior of mothers, both historically and culturally, attracts higher expectations, more intense punishment and blame, and often a pompous self-righteousness. This raises questions about whether even a reasonable observer can really offer sound commentary on the legal and psychological complexities of a case like this. How can most of society understand nuanced issues such as sentencing and intent? What about state of mind? It seems unlikely to me that we can, and I regard most of the commentary as an emotional outpouring of feelings. That’s fine, but let’s be clear about this distinction.
  • Many women say they understand Lindsay’s plight. I’m not sure about that. We are all familiar with being at our wit’s end. Alone. Desperate. Wanting just a minute of peace. Feeling that we are drowning. But do we completely snap?
  • The tragedy shines a light on the mental health epidemic that is contaminating the Western world. We need to give pause and consider where this is heading and how this media frenzy is pouring oil on, rather than relieving, our mental health problem.
  • We all need to honestly examine our reactions and responses to this tragedy and figure out whether we are polarized. And if so, why?

The truth is as mothers we are all pushed to some sort of edge by our children at moments. Not Lindsay’s edge, a fed-up edge. Most of us come back from our edge. We pull through and hopefully learn from it, often shaken and grateful that we can go on.

Three innocent human lives have been eliminated. A family destroyed. A mother ruined, rightly or wrongly.

There are no winners here. As humans, we are all losers.

This is really a time to grieve this loss together rather than hide behind accusations and blame. And to think.

To be human, despite wondering in those minutes whether Lindsay was, and to strive to honor the memory of these children.

item.title: Defunding America's Mental Health Systems
item.description:
Health

Defunding America's Mental Health Systems

We can't fix our mental health care system when there's no data to track it.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Mental health data that helped us realize we are not alone is no longer as available as it was in the past.
  • Just because we cannot measure a problem does not mean that the problem goes away.
  • Even when the data disappears, we can stay grounded in what is real and in front of us.

If you’ve ever felt anxious or depressed and wondered, “Am I the only one struggling these days?” then this post is for you.

There is significant research that demonstrates that misery loves company. We feel just a little bit better knowing others are feeling what we feel, even when what we are feeling is bad.

In the past, we have been able to report data showing rates of anxiety or depression. In fact, it’s one of the greatest advancements in the public health system.

In America, we have the ability to identify rates of anxiety by demographics including age, gender, geographic location, and much more. National surveys report whether rates of depression have increased or decreased, and we use that data to make informed decisions about how to support our communities. We can even use that data to compare what is happening locally with what is happening around the country and the world.

Now, those numbers don’t actually solve all the problems of the world, but they quantify what people are experiencing and help us recognize that what we feel is real.

Sadly, with all that is happening in the world these days, government funding cuts are making access to this important data difficult to find. There are lots of reasons for this, including funding cuts, delays in payments while waiting for lawsuits to resolve issues, staffing changes due to executive orders, and other system interruptions. Some of these interruptions have resulted in data disappearing from government websites only to be reposted later, but with gaps in data.

What makes it difficult is that most of it is happening quietly: one report delayed, one agency disappearing through government restructuring, one website not allowed to report data. It’s almost so discreet that if you’re not paying attention, you could miss it. And then, sadly, when enough data is gone or inaccessible, we realize that we can’t make the case for what is happening among us and how it is making us feel.

Many of us may be feeling uneasy with all that is happening around us, but without the data, it’s hard to quantify why we feel this way. Data offers a tangible explanation, and these days we do not have access to reliable information to help us understand the bigger picture. We talk as a society about the dangers of false information, but we haven't paid enough attention to the dismantling of the systems that collect data.

Why Are We So Unsettled by Not Having Access to the Numbers?

Different people view life experiences differently. What I think is a problem you may think is nothing to be concerned about—until you see the numbers. We welcome these numbers, even when the news is bad, because now we can concretize the problem. Take, for example, the data on loneliness: We are experiencing a loneliness epidemic (definitely bad news), but if I’m someone experiencing loneliness, it makes me feel a little better to know that what I’m experiencing is impacting others the same way.

The biggest problem with what is happening these days is that just because the numbers are no longer available, that doesn’t mean that the problems disappear. Unfortunately, in the absence of numbers, we tend to rely on social media opinions or rumors, which typically result in fear. When we don’t have data, other people’s opinions and assumptions take over, and there is a sense of uncertainty. Not knowing what is happening is often worse than knowing the truth, even when that truth is not good news.

So, What Can We Do About It?

It is really frustrating to know that important information is missing and that there is very little we can do to bring back government databases or conduct cancelled national surveys, but we can be aware of the problem. Once we understand the challenge, here are some things that we can do to support our own mental health in the process.

1. Be aware that your life experiences are real, even if they are not measured on a survey.

While data is important, what we think and feel does not need to be researched in order for it to be true. If you are anxious, depressed, or lonely, your experience matters, and missing statistics do not make it any less real.

2. Look locally and closer to home.

When we don’t have information about what is happening in other places, we can look around us to see what is happening. Spend time talking to people you trust in your own community, look for local support groups, or join community programs. You don’t need statistics to understand what is happening around you.

3. Don’t allow uncertainty to turn into fear.

We know that when reliable information is missing, our brains may want to fill in the blanks. This is when negativity bias kicks in, which means we don’t always find the best explanation. It’s wise to check in with yourself and ask if you know something is bad or if you are just worried that it could be bad. Not knowing the facts may be uncomfortable, but treating fear as the truth is not the solution.

4. It’s important to remember that your voice does matter.

While it’s hard to know what is happening behind the scenes, there are a lot of people working to keep public access to information available. If you are asked to participate in a local survey, choose to share your information, as communities may need to focus on taking care of their own.

When there are opportunities to attend community meetings or support local organizations, show up and participate. Make the effort to tell your local leaders and elected officials what matters to you. Being active in your community will make you feel more connected and like you are contributing.

How I’m Dealing With Lack of Access

This has really had an impact on me as I’ve spent most of my life using data to help people understand that they are not alone. When information is difficult to find, it’s hard for me to envision how I can successfully do my job. What has really helped me is that I am not waiting for the numbers to return. Instead, I’m paying closer attention to the people and communities around me and focusing on what they are saying.

While the numbers are always useful in telling the story, the question remains the same: “How are people really doing?” We can always ask that question and listen to the responses. Losing information definitely makes the world feel less certain, but it doesn’t mean that we can’t figure out how to support each other through difficult times.
